blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Kurtosis measures the tailedness of a distribution: how prone it is to produce extreme values, relative to the Normal distribution. It is computed as b₂ = m₄ ÷ m₂², which equals 3 for a Normal distribution; excess kurtosis is b₂ − 3 (NIST/SEMATECH).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Skewness captures lean to one side. Kurtosis captures something else: how heavy both tails are. Raising deviations to the fourth power makes the few values far from the mean dominate m₄, so kurtosis is driven almost entirely by the tails. Older books describe kurtosis as “peakedness”. That is misleading: kurtosis “tells you virtually nothing about the shape of the peak”; its only clear meaning is tail extremity (Westfall, 2014). A symmetric distribution, with zero skew, can be light-tailed or heavy-tailed.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Heavy-tailed (leptokurtic, excess kurtosis > 0) distributions produce more extreme values than a Normal distribution with the same SD, which matters when you judge whether a Normal-based method is safe. Light-tailed (platykurtic, excess < 0) distributions produce fewer; they often, but not necessarily, look flatter near the centre. Mesokurtic distributions have Normal-like tails (excess ≈ 0).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation: today’s 30 children
blocks.html:
1. m₄ = Σ(x − 11.81)⁴ ÷ 30 = 19.61; m₂ = 2.965, so m₂² = 8.792.
  2. b₂ = 19.61 ÷ 8.792 = 2.23; excess kurtosis = 2.23 − 3 = −0.77.

The weights are mildly platykurtic: the lightest and heaviest children (8.6 and 15.3 kg) are only about 1.8 and 2.0 SDs from the mean, so there are no long tails. Software often reports an adjusted sample excess kurtosis (−0.68 here), so check which definition a program uses.

points.html: b₂ = m₄ ÷ m₂²; Normal = 3; excess kurtosis = b₂ − 3. Many sources and programs say “kurtosis” when they mean excess kurtosis.
Leptokurtic = heavier tails than Normal; platykurtic = lighter; mesokurtic = Normal-like. Kurtosis describes tails, not the peak.
Skewness and kurtosis are descriptive signals, not a pass/fail test of normality. Combine them with a histogram, a Q-Q plot and, where relevant, a formal normality test (all in §9.3).

questions.prompt: You want to compare how variable height is with how variable weight is in the same children. Why can’t you compare raw SDs, and what do you compare instead? Compute it for heights with mean 85 cm, SD 4 cm and weights with mean 11.8 kg, SD 1.75 kg.
questions.answer: The SDs are in different units (cm and kg) and on different scales, so their sizes cannot be compared. Compare coefficients of variation, which are unit-free. Height: CV = 4 ÷ 85 × 100 = 4.7%. Weight: CV = 1.75 ÷ 11.8 × 100 = 14.8%. Relative to its own mean, weight is about three times as variable as height.

questions.prompt: Describe a right-skewed distribution of hospital length of stay, and state the usual order of mean, median and mode. In one ward the mean stay is 6 days, the median 5 days and the SD 4 days: compute Pearson’s coefficient of skewness and the mode implied by the empirical relation.
questions.answer: Most patients cluster at short stays, and a long tail stretches toward a few very long stays. For such a unimodal right-skewed curve the order is usually mode < median < mean: the mean is pulled toward the tail. This is a rule of thumb that can fail, especially for discrete data such as whole days. Pearson Sk = 3(mean − median) ÷ SD = 3 × (6 − 5) ÷ 4 = 0.75 (positive: right skew). Empirical mode ≈ 3 × median − 2 × mean = 15 − 12 = 3 days.

questions.prompt: A colleague says a platykurtic distribution “must have a flat top”. Is that right? Explain what kurtosis actually measures.
questions.answer: No. Kurtosis, b₂ = m₄ ÷ m₂², is dominated by the fourth powers of the largest deviations, so it measures tail extremity: how prone the distribution is to extreme values relative to a Normal distribution (b₂ = 3). A platykurtic distribution (excess kurtosis < 0) has lighter tails than Normal. It often looks flatter near the centre, but it need not; the peak’s shape contributes little to kurtosis (Westfall, 2014).
